Pointing toward an oath without actually swearing it is more forceful, and this forcefulness is what is intended here. In this manner the purpose is well achieved, and this style is repeated again and again in the Holy Qur'an. After this, the reality of the Resurrection and the reality of the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah) are then explained.

Regarding the reality of the Resurrection, the matter is mentioned repeatedly in this Surah. But what is the nafs al-lawwamah? Several sayings are recorded about it in the transmitted tafsirs (tafsir ma'thur). It is narrated from Hasan al-Basri, who said: "Whenever you see a truthful person, he will always reproach himself: 'What did I mean by my words? What is the purpose of my eating? And what is the benefit of my speech?' As for the wicked (fajir), he keeps advancing on his path and never reproaches himself at any stage."

It is also narrated from Hasan that none among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth will fail to reproach himself on the Day of Resurrection.

It is narrated from Ikrimah that on both good and evil you will blame one another, saying, "Would that I had done such and such!" The same narration is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it means the nafs al-lawwamah, and from him also that it is the self that is blamed for a blameworthy matter. It is narrated from Mujahid that every soul that regrets the matters that have passed and reproaches itself. Qatadah says the lawwamah is the soul that commits fujur (wickedness). Ibn Jarir says: "All these sayings are close in meaning, and the closer meaning is that by the nafs al-lawwamah is meant the soul that reproaches itself for good and for evil, and regrets the good that it failed to do."

In our view, the saying of Hasan al-Basri is better: the nafs al-lawwamah is the one that reproaches itself, saying: "By God, whenever you see a believer, he is always reproaching himself: what was the purpose of the words I spoke? What was the purpose of what I ate, and what was the purpose of what I thought?" And the corrupt and the wicked simply keeps advancing, and does not reproach himself for any of his matters.

So the nafs al-lawwamah is the one that is awake, possesses the fear of God, is constantly cautious and keeps its own account, watches its environment, keeps watch over its desires, and is always careful lest it be deceived. This soul stands in contrast to the nafs al-fajirah. The nafs al-fajirah is the soul that keeps advancing, lost in wickedness and immorality, whose attributes are that it lies, turns away, and with great arrogance turns to its kin and associates, and does not hold itself to account.

"Lā uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamah, wa-lā uqsimu bi-al-nafs al-lawwamah" (75:1-2): "I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection, and I do not swear by the self-reproaching soul." That is, an oath is not being sworn regarding the occurrence of the Resurrection. Here God has negated the swearing of an oath and has also omitted what matter the oath is not being sworn upon; yet the matter about which the oath is being sworn is mentioned in another manner. As if this is a new statement with no connection to the oath.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 75, verse 3:

"Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, indeed! We are able to put together even his fingertips" (75:3-4). The Makkan polytheists were gripped by a conscious doubt: how could scattered old bones be gathered together and made into a human being again, when they had been crushed into fragments, mixed with the dust, and scattered across the earth? How could a person be raised again in exactly the same form? This doubt still lingers in some hearts to this day. The Noble Qur'an refutes it with the utmost emphasis: yes, it will indeed happen, and it will certainly happen.

Nay, We are able to restore even his fingertips [Qur'an 75:4]: "Why not? We are capable of making his fingers complete down to their very tips." Banan means the extremities of the fingers. The emphasis in the meaning is created this way: We would restore the bones down to their finest parts, and when One who can make each individual fingertip whole, what difficulty is there in gathering the bones together? The purpose is that every single part of a human being will be reassembled and no part will be left behind. The whole person will be present, whether the part is small or large.

Here the matter has been stated in this way, but at the end of the surah another argument for resurrection is also brought forward. Here, only their doubt and its apparent cause have been expressed, namely that these people do not expect the bones to be gathered together. In truth, a human being desires wickedness and immorality, and wishes to keep advancing in that wickedness and immorality, with nothing to stop him, and without having to face any reckoning or any reward or punishment. For this reason he regards the occurrence of the Resurrection as far-fetched and seeks a way to escape from its occurrence.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 75, verses 5–6:

Rather, man wishes to continue committing wrongdoing ahead of him. He asks: "When will that Day of Resurrection come?" Here the question is taken from the word "ayyan" (when). This word is emphasized and melodious, and this emphasis and melody in fact point to the fact that these people think about when the Resurrection will come, and this thought is for them so that they keep advancing in immorality and debauchery, and so that the concept of being raised after death and of accountability cannot stop them, nor can it disturb their lives. In truth, the concept of the Hereafter is the one thing that can curb this kind of feeling, and can restrain the lovers of immorality and debauchery. Such people want to continue these obstacles-free and unrestrained bonds of immorality and debauchery.

The denial of the occurrence of the Resurrection, and the view that it is far-fetched, is answered here very swiftly, in a decisive manner, and in such a way that no doubt remains. In this answer, human senses, human consciousness and cosmic observation are presented.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 75, verse 10:

Ayna al-mafarr (75:10): "Where is the place of escape?" And in this state of anguish and panic, a person will run about in every direction, just as a mouse, when it is shut inside a cage, keeps running around in every direction. Now there is no place to flee to, no place of refuge, and one can neither go forward nor go back.

"Nay, [there is] no refuge (wazar)..." — translating the passage as given:

Quran 75:11–12: "No! There is no refuge. Unto your Lord, on that Day, will be the place of rest (al-mustaqarr)." The Urdu text quotes: "Hargiz nahin, wahan koi jaye panah na hogi, is roz tere Rab hi ke samne jakar thaharna hoga."

Translation of the commentary:

On that Day, the situation will not be what man wishes, namely that he may advance without reckoning or accountability along the path of immorality and wickedness, with no one to question him. Rather, on that Day there will be a full and thorough accounting, and he will be questioned about the deeds he had forgotten. And when he remembers, then there will be recompense and punishment.

"Nay, [there is] no refuge (wazar)..." — translating the passage as given:

Quran 75:11–12: "No! There is no refuge. Unto your Lord, on that Day, will be the place of rest (al-mustaqarr)." The Urdu text quotes: "Hargiz nahin, wahan koi jaye panah na hogi, is roz tere Rab hi ke samne jakar thaharna hoga."

Translation of the commentary:

On that Day, the situation will not be what man wishes, namely that he may advance without reckoning or accountability along the path of immorality and wickedness, with no one to question him. Rather, on that Day there will be a full and thorough accounting, and he will be questioned about the deeds he had forgotten. And when he remembers, then there will be recompense and punishment.

On that Day man will be informed of what he sent ahead and what he left behind. That is, the deeds he performed before his death and the traces he left after his death, whether they were good traces or bad, because some of a person's deeds have effects that remain and keep adding to his account.

Then, on that Day, man will put forward excuses, but none of his excuses will be accepted, because he is responsible for what he did. Allah has guided the human soul to good and evil. If the soul leads a person to good, the end will be good, and if it leads him to evil, he will be called to account for it.

Nay, man is a witness against himself, even though he may put forward his excuses. (75:14–15)

It is worth noting here that in this surah everything moves at an extremely rapid pace. The phrases, the rhyme, the music and cadence, the scenes and their vivid brightness, and likewise the reckoning, will all proceed swiftly. Everything, the first and the last, will be laid bare before them, and this is because they used to ask when the Day would come and regarded the Resurrection as very distant and very impossible.

Now four verses follow which give you guidance regarding the Qur'an, and they are a parenthetical digression (jumla mu'taridah).

Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We recite it, follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its explanation (bayan).

Regarding these verses, what we have said in the introduction to the surah must be supplemented by this: Allah has taken upon Himself absolutely the task of preserving and safeguarding the Qur'an. Allah is the guarantor that the Qur'an will remain alive, will remain preserved, its collection and compilation (jam' wa tadwin) will be completed, and Allah Himself will also provide its explanation (tashrih). The full responsibility rests with Allah. The responsibility of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is only that he receive it and convey it to the people. This was said because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would become eager to receive the revelation, and he wanted to take in and memorize the entire Qur'an quickly, and he was extremely earnest that not a single word of it be left out. Therefore he would repeat it hurriedly, so he was given this guidance that he should not try to repeat it with his tongue; the preservation is Allah's responsibility.

This matter has been recorded in several places in the Qur'an, because Allah the Exalted wanted to fix in the minds of the Muslims that the memorization and collection of the Qur'an is very important, to which we have alluded in the introduction to the surah.

After this parenthetical digression, the surah now presents the scenes of the Resurrection, showing what the self that blames (nafs lawwamah) will be like in them. In these scenes it is recalled that what desires arise in your souls concerning this world, how you are absorbed in this world and have forgotten the Hereafter, and do not care for the Hereafter at all. Just see what your plight is going to be there. In a very vivid and dynamic scene, this condition is placed before humankind, one that is extremely impactful and suggestive.

Now the Qur'an presents a vivid scene, which is a unique style of the Qur'an.

﴿Some faces on that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ (75:22-23). This verse points, in the form of a glimpse, to a state for which no human being can find words; nor can a person truly grasp that state. This is such a picture of the condition of the successful and fortunate people that it cannot be depicted in full through circumstances; rather, in comparison with that state even Paradise loses its reality, though it is filled with every kind of blessing. This state, that these faces will be fresh and will be looking toward their Lord, means looking toward their Lord with delight and contentment. This is the highest station of felicity!

In this world, a person sometimes takes great delight in the beauty found in the universe and within the human soul. A person, for example, is lost in a moonlit night. If there is no moonlight, even a dark night has its own pleasure. Then the dawn breaking forth shows its beauty. The long and deep shadows of trees, the successive waves of the sea, the valleys of deserts, the greenery of gardens, beautiful fruits and flowers, hearts full of joy, moments of firm faith, overcoming difficulties, and other beauties with which this world is adorned, from which a person continues to derive pleasure, and with the wings of imagination and light he runs and flies about in this world. He finds such joy and delight that he forgets the pains and sorrows of life and forgets worldly and physical pleasures. The desires of the self, material longings and pleasures are for a moment removed from the mind.

But what would be the state of his joy when he goes beyond the perfection and beauty created by Allah and sees the attributes of the Divine Being, with his gaze fixed upon Allah.

The truth is that this station is attained when the special help of Allah is with a person; then it is attained when someone receives steadfastness from Allah. People gain control over themselves, they possess firmness, and they enjoy the felicity of the Hereafter, a felicity that cannot be described and whose reality is difficult to fully comprehend.

﴿Some faces on that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ (75:22-23). Why would they not be radiant, when they are looking toward their Lord?

A person in this world beholds the creations of Allah: beautiful fruits, wondrous flowers, brightly colored and beautiful birds and their feathers, beautiful souls and good deeds; on seeing these things his heart rejoices, the joy shows on his face, and his face becomes fresh. But if a person is looking toward the majesty, beauty and light of Allah's Essence, then what can be said of his joy and good fortune? A person can reach this station only when he throws away with a single jolt all the obstacles that prevent him from reaching this lofty station. This station can be attained only when a person removes all defects from himself and from his environment, and he is looking at nothing but Allah.

How will a person look at Allah? With which organ will he see? Will he have the faculty of sight? What will be the means of seeing Allah? These are matters beyond our imagination. It is an idea given to the believing heart, a grace from which the believing soul will benefit. It is a pure and clear grace of felicity, free from the pollutions of the world, that the believer will receive.

As for the rationalists, instead of deriving joy and delight from this, they begin disputes over such verses. They gain nothing from it, and just as they are deprived of joy and contentment, they are likewise deprived of understanding and comprehension. This is because the matters of that world cannot be known by the ordinary intellect of this world, but by the perceiving faculty of faith.

The development of the human personality, and its separation and elevation from the limited earthly personality, is what can connect it on the Day of Resurrection with the unlimited personality and the exalted, supreme Being. Without this, it is difficult for a human being to conceive how one can be united with the unlimited. Therefore the lengthy debates that took place between the Mu'tazilah and the Ahl as-Sunnah regarding the vision of Allah were entirely fruitless, because there will be a difference between this earthly personality of man and his personality in the Hereafter.

We can understand the words of Allah only in the sense that fits within our limited self; when our personality itself changes and rises above these limited conceptions, then the nature and meaning of these words will change too. Words are in reality symbols for the meanings that exist in human conception. When the limits and constraints of human conception change, the meanings of words will change too. When the human personality changes, and the power of its perceiving faculty changes, then along with it words and concepts both will change. In this world we understand these words in the sense that fits our present state. Therefore we should not get entangled in meanings that we cannot derive from these words.

So we should only hope for that felicity and that sacred joy and delight which we can conceive in terms of the meanings of this world, and we should keep our gaze raised toward the higher realm for such graces. And there is no greater delight than this.

But what would be the state of his joy when he goes beyond the perfection and beauty created by Allah and sees the attributes of the Divine Being, with his gaze fixed upon Allah.

The truth is that this station is attained when the special help of Allah is with a person; then it is attained when someone receives steadfastness from Allah. People gain control over themselves, they possess firmness, and they enjoy the felicity of the Hereafter, a felicity that cannot be described and whose reality is difficult to fully comprehend.

﴿Some faces on that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ (75:22-23). Why would they not be radiant, when they are looking toward their Lord?

A person in this world beholds the creations of Allah: beautiful fruits, wondrous flowers, brightly colored and beautiful birds and their feathers, beautiful souls and good deeds; on seeing these things his heart rejoices, the joy shows on his face, and his face becomes fresh. But if a person is looking toward the majesty, beauty and light of Allah's Essence, then what can be said of his joy and good fortune? A person can reach this station only when he throws away with a single jolt all the obstacles that prevent him from reaching this lofty station. This station can be attained only when a person removes all defects from himself and from his environment, and he is looking at nothing but Allah.

How will a person look at Allah? With which organ will he see? Will he have the faculty of sight? What will be the means of seeing Allah? These are matters beyond our imagination. It is an idea given to the believing heart, a grace from which the believing soul will benefit. It is a pure and clear grace of felicity, free from the pollutions of the world, that the believer will receive.

As for the rationalists, instead of deriving joy and delight from this, they begin disputes over such verses. They gain nothing from it, and just as they are deprived of joy and contentment, they are likewise deprived of understanding and comprehension. This is because the matters of that world cannot be known by the ordinary intellect of this world, but by the perceiving faculty of faith.

The development of the human personality, and its separation and elevation from the limited earthly personality, is what can connect it on the Day of Resurrection with the unlimited personality and the exalted, supreme Being. Without this, it is difficult for a human being to conceive how one can be united with the unlimited. Therefore the lengthy debates that took place between the Mu'tazilah and the Ahl as-Sunnah regarding the vision of Allah were entirely fruitless, because there will be a difference between this earthly personality of man and his personality in the Hereafter.

We can understand the words of Allah only in the sense that fits within our limited self; when our personality itself changes and rises above these limited conceptions, then the nature and meaning of these words will change too. Words are in reality symbols for the meanings that exist in human conception. When the limits and constraints of human conception change, the meanings of words will change too. When the human personality changes, and the power of its perceiving faculty changes, then along with it words and concepts both will change. In this world we understand these words in the sense that fits our present state. Therefore we should not get entangled in meanings that we cannot derive from these words.

So we should only hope for that felicity and that sacred joy and delight which we can conceive in terms of the meanings of this world, and we should keep our gaze raised toward the higher realm for such graces. And there is no greater delight than this.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 75, verses 24–25:

"Some faces on that Day will be downcast, thinking that a backbreaking calamity is about to befall them." (75:24–25)

Who are these faces? They are the faces that will be troubled, wretched and blackened. They will be deprived of and despairing of the mercy-filled gaze of Allah. This deprivation will be due to their own mistakes and backwardness, due to their materialism and lack of insight. Grief and sorrow will be hidden upon their faces, and because of that grief and sorrow, darkness will have spread over their faces. For they will be seized by the intense fear that they are very soon to be struck by an event that will break their backs.

Faqirah (فاقرة) refers to the spinal column. Here it means fear, dread, restlessness, the blackening of the face, anxiety, and grief and sorrow.

This is the picture of the Hereafter which these people cast behind their backs and leave neglected, while they run after the brief life of this world, which they value greatly. Yet the Day that is coming is of great importance. The true outcome will be decided there, and there is a vast difference between the importance of this world and that of the Hereafter. On the Day of Resurrection, some faces will be fresh and radiant, looking toward their Lord, while other faces will be downcast and will fear that a backbreaking calamity is about to strike them.

The scenes of the Resurrection are such that eyes will be fixed in stillness, the moon will lose its light, the sun and moon will be brought together, and man will cry out helplessly, "Where can I flee?" Then the ends of people there will be very different, and there will be long distances between the fate of the people of Paradise and the people of Hell. The faces of the people of Paradise will be fresh, gazing upon their Lord, while the faces of the people of Hell will be dark, and they will be about to be struck by intense calamity.

These are scenes of great emotional impact, and the true power of their effect lies in their style of expression. It is a vivid, picturing, living style. Continuing these scenes and witnesses, there is now brought forward a scene that is an everyday one, which we see with our own eyes. It is a heavy and unpleasant scene, yet it is inevitable and occurs in every place and every house.

This scene is the scene of death: that death which every living being must face, and from which no person can keep himself far, nor can he save anyone else from it. This death separates the closest of friends. It goes on its own path and is ever continuing. At no moment does its occurrence pause. The weeping of someone and the wailing of another have no effect on it. Nor do the regrets of those who are separated have any effect on it, nor does someone's love have any effect on it, nor does anyone's fear have any effect on it. This death seizes tyrants and oppressors in the same way that it seizes an insect. It annihilates the rich and the poor, slaves and dictators alike. This death, against which man has no stratagem or remedy, yet alas, people rarely think about it, about how great the overpowering force of death is.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 75, verse 30:

"Ila..." to "al-masaq" (75:30): "That Day, the drawing near will be to your Lord." This scene is so vivid and dynamic that a person sees it as though a train is moving along. Every word depicts a movement; every moment and every pause reveals hurrying and motion. As death draws near, the people's movement and wailing and lamentation intensify. This is a bitter reality towards which the whole gathering is advancing, and against it all remedies have failed. And then comes the final scene.

"Ila Rabbika..." to "al-masaq" (75:30): "It is indeed the day of drawing near to your Lord." Now the curtain falls, but the picture remains fixed on the screen of our imagination. Indelible impressions are settled upon our feelings. Now there is a dreadful silence over the atmosphere; here and there the sound of weeping is heard.

Before this living, real and undeniable scene, there is now also a portrait of those who deny, and of the heedless and the negligent. These are the people who are deprived of felicity because they neither act nor obey. In their lap there is nothing but sins and acts of disobedience, and these people are occupied in play and frivolity and are absorbed in this state of theirs.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 75, verses 31–33:

It is related in the narrations that these verses were revealed concerning a particular person. In some narrations his name is also mentioned: that he was ʿAmr ibn Hisham, Abu Jahl. This man would sometimes come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), listen to the Qur'an, and then leave, without believing, without obeying him, without fearing Allah, and without adopting a respectful attitude. Rather, he would go on to cause the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) further harm, speaking ill of him and preventing people from entering the religion of Islam. Then he would swagger over these deeds of his and take pride in his exploits, as is stated in this verse.

Here the Qur'an mocks this man and makes a most contemptuous remark. The Qur'an describes this man's act of arrogance with the word yatamattā (75:33), that is, swaggering while arching his back, and displaying a heavy kind of disdain in which the signs of aversion are plainly visible.

Leaving aside any particular individual, in every age there is an Abu Jahl who opposes the truth. He hears, he understands, yet he turns away, and he displays great cleverness in diverting people from the path of Allah. He harms the callers to truth, and he engages in great schemes of deception. He turns away and takes pride in his mischief, although in reality such a person spreads corruption on the earth and blocks the path of truth, righteousness and reform.

He turns away and takes pride in his mischief, although in reality such a person spreads corruption on the earth and blocks the path of truth, righteousness and reform.

This is a common idiomatic expression in the Arabic manner of speech, but it also carries a warning and a threat. Once, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seized Abu Jahl by the throat and said: "Woe to you, and woe again" (Ouly laka fa-ouly, 75:34–35 / 57:53 as cited). Then that enemy of Allah said: "Muhammad, do you threaten me? By Allah, neither you nor your Lord can harm me, and I am more honourable than all the people who have ever walked between the two mountains of Makkah." So Allah seized him on the day of Badr, and thus Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Lord of Muhammad (ﷺ) ruined all his schemes.

Before Abu Jahl, Pharaoh too had said to his people: "I know of no god for you other than myself" ("Ma 'alimtu lakum min ilahin ghayri," – "I do not find for you any ruler other than me"). And he said: "Does the kingdom of Egypt not belong to me, and do these rivers not flow beneath me?"

Many Abu Jahls have passed, who committed crimes against the Islamic call relying on their tribes, their strength and their people, considered themselves something of importance, and had forgotten Allah; yet Allah destroyed and ruined them through gnats and flies. In any case, the destruction of every Pharaoh has a fixed appointed time, from which there is neither advance nor delay.

Finally, another important reality from people's lives is brought forward. This reality also points to life after death, which they stubbornly denied. And from it there also becomes apparent the wise planning and destiny of their own life's growth, and the wondrous and lesson-giving technology created by God, which demands that the Resurrection will certainly occur; and the study of life itself makes the occurrence of resurrection and gathering necessary, provided that someone studies it with a seeing eye.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 75, verse 36:

This is the final section, which is extremely impactful, and in it there are allusions to profound realities. Regarding these realities, the audience of that time had never even reflected. Among these realities, more than anything, there are indications of the creation of man and of the arrangements for the development of his life in this world.

"Does man think that he will be left neglected?" (75:36). The Arabs regarded life as a movement that had neither a cause nor a reason, neither a purpose nor an end. People were born from their mothers' wombs and went into graves, and the period between birth and death was reserved for play and amusement. Life consisted of adornment, embellishment, and mutual boasting and pride. People spent their lives in the same way that animals do. That this universe has a natural order, that life has a purpose, and that it has come into existence under a wisdom, these matters were beyond their understanding. They did not think that man has been created according to a fixed destiny, that he is a responsible creature, and that behind his creation there is a system of reward and punishment, and that this journey of life is a test. As for the notion that this life is a purposeful life, that behind it stands an all-powerful Being who is the Lord of the worlds, and that He has created everything according to a measure and a wisdom, and that everything is destined to reach an end, these concepts were not in their thinking; rather, these people were far removed from such concepts. The condition of the Arabs in the age before Islam was exactly like this.

Yet the very difference between man and animal lies in this awareness: that events occur under a purpose, and their goals and aims are determined. Just as this whole universe is purposeful, so too is Man purposeful within it. As this awareness of man has progressed, humanity has advanced; under this awareness, human life becomes interconnected. Under this concept, man keeps account of the moments of his life, reflects upon all incidents and events, keeps the present and future connected with the past, then keeps this whole life connected with the system of this universe, and then connects man and the entire universe with the Divine Being, so that this man, his life, and this world have not been created in vain.

This is that great outlook on life to which the Qur'an brought people. It was a great revolutionary concept. If one considers the thinking generally prevalent among people at that time, then in comparison with it this was a highly revolutionary thought. Moreover, compared with the philosophies and ideas then current and prevalent in the world, this belief and outlook was a revolutionary concept and thought. (See my book Islam, the Universe, Life and Man.)

This is the point: "Does man think that he will be left neglected?" (75:36). This is in fact one of those few Qur'anic indications that guide man to establish connections and relationships with this universe. They define a purpose and an aim for this world and for man. They establish causes and means for events, and they designate certain things as the results of others. Thus this whole universe, and man within it, become purposeful and interconnected.

Here, arguments for this concept are presented that are extremely simple and direct, and there is no difficulty in understanding them. In summary: man is not unbridled and purposeless.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 75, verses 37–38:

Alam yak ................ yumni (37) Thumma ................ fasawwa (38) Fa-ja'ala ........................ (39) (75:37–39) "Was he not a drop of fluid semen that is emitted (into the womb)? Then he became a clot of blood, then Allah created his body and made his limbs proportionate, then from him He made two kinds, male and female."

What is this human being? From what was he created? How was he, and how did he become what he is? And where did this journey of life begin, and where has it reached? How did he arrive on this earth, which is a small star?

Was he not a small drop of water, a single drop of fluid that is emitted? Was not the human being an extremely minute speck visible only under a microscope? Then he became a single cell. Then he became a particular clot of blood. This clot kept growing in the womb of the mother. At first it remained suspended from the walls of the womb and drew its nourishment from the blood there. Who taught him all these stages of this journey? Who gave him this power, and who showed him this path?

After that, who gave him the form of a foetus, in which the powers within became balanced and whose organs became harmonious and proportionate with one another? Then how did this single cell take on the form of many millions of cells? Although at first it was a single cell and a microscopic egg, the journey and transformation that this cell covered up to the stage of a foetus was longer than the stages from birth to death. The question is: who is it that is preparing him for these long transformations, although at the beginning he was an extremely small creature? He had neither intellect nor powers of perception within him, nor did he have worldly experience.

Then how did Allah create male and female from one and the same creature? Does this creature itself shape itself into the form of male or female? Does this creature itself decide to become male or female, or is it some other power that makes it male or female in those darknesses?

The truth is that no problem of this universe can be solved except by conceiving of a Being who is All-Powerful, who is the Governor, who is the first cause of all events and occurrences, and who possesses absolute power. It is that very Being who brings the human being from a microscopic particle to this stage.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 75, verses 39–40:

﴿Then He made of him two kinds, the male and the female.﴾ (75:39) Then from him He made two kinds, male and female.

This fact, which clings to human consciousness, is then summarized in this way, and the conclusion is drawn from all these truths as follows.

﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ (75:40) "Is He not able to bring the dead back to life?" Yes, indeed Allah is able to bring the dead back to life. Yes, Allah is also able to raise everyone on the Day of Gathering and Dispersal. Yes, it is a truth that man is compelled to believe in the doctrine of the Hereafter, because this entire universe bears witness to it.

Thus this Surah ends with a powerful statement, whose effect on the veils of thought and feeling is extremely deep and decisive, and a person draws closer to this universe, its reality, and the Governing Being working behind it.
